items.title: penguineer
items.text:
penguineer finds the root cause of off-spec lots from historian and LIMS exports, on a laptop and offline. It is a KausalFlow open-source project under the Apache-2.0 license.

It reads files and writes files. The engines are deterministic Python, and an LLM is optional and never decides a ranking. Every command is defined once, as a Pydantic parameter model, a result model and a function. The CLI, the --json output and the Python API are all generated from that definition, so they cannot drift apart.

Alchemist imports penguineer as a library and adds the UI, runners, project management, the data catalog, staging and sealing on top. penguineer has none of those itself.

Status

This is an early release. init, data health, graph check, graph draft, graph lags, lag, investigate, bench homeostat and mcp work. graph draft reads tag names and DEXPI P&IDs, and can ask an LLM for the relations they leave open.

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• Getting started: install it and run data health on the demo plant.
  • Commands and run records: how one definition becomes the CLI and the Python API.
  • Homeostat Live: run on a public simulated plant.
  • MCP server: let an assistant such as Claude Code run the commands.
  • CLI reference: every command and option.

items.title: Contributing
items.text:
uv sync
uv run pytest
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .

items.title: Adding a command
items.text:
1. Add a module in src/penguineer/commands/ with a Params model (subclass CommandParams), a Result model (subclass CommandResult) and a function decorated with @command("group name", params=..., result=...). Its docstring is the help text.
  2. Import the module in src/penguineer/commands/__init__.py.

  3. Regenerate the schema snapshot and the CLI reference:

    PENGUINEER_UPDATE_SCHEMAS=1 uv run pytest tests/test_schemas.py
uv run python scripts/gen_cli_reference.py

Use FilePath for input files, so the CLI checks that they exist and the run record hashes them. Put engines in engines/, typed in and out and free of global state.

items.title: Schemas are public API
items.text: tests/test_schemas.py fails when any command's Params or Result schema changes, because Alchemist builds on them. Regenerate the snapshot only for an intended change, and say so in the pull request.

items.title: The bench and the calibration
items.text:
A change to a test, a rule or the ranking changes how investigate scores on the homeostat bench; the Bench workflow posts the smoke bench in every pull request's job summary. To refit the weights and thresholds after such a change:

uv sync --extra bench
uv run penguineer bench homeostat --scenarios train --per-fault 12 --project .
uv run penguineer bench homeostat --scenarios validation --per-fault 12 --project .
uv run python scripts/fit_calibration.py .penguineer/bench/train-* .penguineer/bench/validation-*

Commit the new src/penguineer/engines/calibration.json with the change, and quote the validation numbers in the pull request. Never fit on the validation split's answers beyond the thresholds, and never on the hidden split.

A change to penguineer lag's engine (engines/lagfit.py) is checked the same way against Homeostat plants with known volumes: run scripts/validate_lag.py (see Finding the actual lag) and quote its errors in the pull request.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
The site is built with Zensical:

uvx zensical serve    # preview on http://localhost:8000
uvx zensical build    # static site in ./site

docs/reference/cli.md is generated from the registry, and a test fails when it is out of date.

items.title: Docs previews and screenshots
items.text:
Every pull request from a branch of this repository gets a preview of the documentation at https://kausalflow.com/penguineer/pr-preview/pr-<number>/, posted as a comment on the pull request and removed when it closes. main is published at https://kausalflow.com/penguineer/. Both come from the gh-pages branch, written by .github/workflows/docs.yml.

Each deploy also has screenshots of every page under _screenshots/ (for a preview, pr-preview/pr-<number>/_screenshots/), taken with Playwright by scripts/screenshot_docs.py. To take them locally:

uvx zensical==0.0.70 build --clean
uv run --no-project --with playwright==1.56.0 python scripts/screenshot_docs.py site

A pull request description includes the preview link and screenshots of the pages it changes, and of any visible output such as a command's summary. The pull request template has sections for both.

items.title: Releasing
items.text:
penguineer and plantgraph are published to PyPI together, with one version. .github/workflows/release.yml builds both, installs the wheels in a clean environment, and publishes them with PyPI trusted publishing when a GitHub release is published. No token is stored in the repository.

  1. Run the release gate: start the Release gate workflow from the Actions tab on main. It runs the bench on the hidden split (160 plants by default) with the seed in the repository secret BENCH_HIDDEN_SEED, and passes when the scores meet the gate in The homeostat bench. It shows only the summary scores and uploads nothing, because this repository is public.
  2. Set the new version in pyproject.toml, in packages/plantgraph/pyproject.toml, and in penguineer's plantgraph== pin (tests/test_versions.py checks that the three agree), then run uv lock. Merge that to main.
  3. On GitHub, create a release from main with the tag v<version>, for example v0.1.0. The workflow stops if the tag does not match the version.

If publishing fails part way (for example PyPI errors after uploading one of the two packages), run the Release workflow by hand from the Actions tab with the release tag as input. Files already on PyPI are skipped.

PyPI side, done once per project: add a trusted publisher with owner kausalflow, repository penguineer and workflow release.yml, with environment pypi for penguineer and pypi-plantgraph for plantgraph. Before a project's first release, add it as a pending publisher under Your account > Publishing. The two environments differ on purpose: PyPI cannot create a new project with a token that already matches an existing project's publisher.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
penguineer needs Python 3.11 or newer. It is on PyPI:

uv tool install penguineer   # or: pip install penguineer
penguineer --help

The examples on this page use the demo plant in the repository, so clone it and run penguineer from the checkout with uv:

git clone https://github.com/kausalflow/penguineer
cd penguineer
uv sync
uv run penguineer --help

items.title: Check the demo plant's data
items.text:
examples/demo/ holds twelve hours of one-minute data from a small reactor, with four data faults injected on purpose (see scripts/make_demo_data.py), and its plant graph.

uv run penguineer data health \
  --data examples/demo/historian.csv \
  --graph examples/demo/graph.yaml

data health: 5 tags, 3555 samples, 2026-08-03 00:00 to 2026-08-03 11:59 UTC
findings: 4 (1 critical, 3 warning, 0 info)

  critical PI-103.PV  out_of_range 2026-08-03 09:30  outside instrument range [0, 10]: min 10.918, max 11.114
  warning  AI-201.PV  spike        2026-08-03 08:15  spike of 2.5293 from 3.2329
  warning  FI-102.PV  gap          2026-08-03 05:59  no samples for 46 min (usual period 60 s)
  warning  TI-101.PV  flatline     2026-08-03 03:00  value frozen at 180.585 for 2.0 h

The setpoint FIC-102.SP is constant all day and is not reported, because the graph says it is a setpoint.

Each run writes runs/<run_id>/run.json and health.json under the project folder (--project, default the current folder). Add --json to print the result model instead of the summary.

items.title: Investigate an off-spec lot
items.text:
examples/offspec/ holds three days of a small plant in which lot L0803-A came out low on purity. Its cause is known: the feed preheater fouled.

uv run penguineer investigate --lot L0803-A \
  --lims examples/offspec/lims.csv --data examples/offspec/historian.csv \
  --graph examples/offspec/graph.yaml --lots examples/offspec/lots.csv

The preheater outlet temperature TI-101 comes first, with high confidence. The report lands in reports/<run_id>/report.html; here is that report, and Investigating an off-spec lot explains each step.

items.title: Start a project for your own unit
items.text:
uv run penguineer init --project my-unit

This creates penguineer.yaml, an empty graph.yaml, and the folders data/, runs/, reports/ and .penguineer/cache/. Put your historian exports in data/ and describe the plant in graph.yaml (see The plant graph).

Next, try a real simulated plant: Homeostat Live.

items.title: The homeostat bench
items.text:
penguineer bench homeostat measures how often investigate names the right root cause. It generates plants with Homeostat, injects one known fault into each, exports what a plant would export (historian, LIMS, lots, the plant graph), runs investigate on the first off-spec lot exactly as it runs on a real plant, and only then reads the answer.

pip install "penguineer[bench]"
penguineer bench homeostat --scenarios validation --per-fault 12

bench homeostat: 85 validation scenarios (11 plants skipped: no lot off spec)

  hit@1                 89%
  hit@3                 96%  (95% 90% to 99%)
  wrong-confident rate  5%
  data-fault catch rate 95%

  fault type              n  hit@1  hit@3
  catalyst_loss          12    92%   100%
  feed_b_flow            10    80%   100%
  feed_flow               7   100%   100%
  feed_property          12    83%   100%
  reactor_fouling        12    83%    83%
  reactor_sensor_bias    12    92%    92%
  reactor_sensor_drift    8   100%   100%
  reactor_setpoint       12    92%   100%

The first run generates the scenarios, which takes a few minutes per fault type while Homeostat compiles each plant; later runs reuse them from .penguineer/bench/ in the project. --bundles runs on bundles you already have, and bench.json and scenarios.csv in the run folder hold every scenario's result.

items.title: The bench plant
items.text:
A small continuous reactor train, defined in src/penguineer/bench/plant.py:

Node What it is Tags S-A, S-B Two feeds FT-101, FT-102 (flowmeters) M-101 Feed mixer; its outlet composition sets the reactor's feed ratio AT-101 (online analyzer) S-mix, E-201 The mixed feed and its heater, loop TIC-201 TT-200 (inlet temperature), TT-201, TIC-201 setpoint and output R-301 The reactor, loop TIC-301; the product property follows an Arrhenius law in its temperature, a power of the feed ratio and the catalyst activity TT-301, TIC-301 setpoint and output S-product, SP-1 The product and its sample point lab result every 4 hours, reported an hour later

Each drawn plant differs in its volumes, its kinetics and its noise, and runs for three days: two grades alternate in the first day, and the fault arrives between hours 40 and 56. The graph each bundle carries is the true one, with dead times from the drawn volumes. Spec limits come from the in-control lots before the fault. A plant where no lot goes off spec is skipped: the fault was too small to matter, so it is neither a hit nor a miss.

items.title: The faults
items.text:
Fault type What happens Counts as found when a hypothesis names feed_property Feed B's composition steps up AT-101, M-101 or S-B feed_flow Feed A's flow rises FT-101 or S-A feed_b_flow Feed B's flow drops FT-102 or S-B reactor_setpoint The reactor setpoint is lowered the TIC-301 setpoint change reactor_fouling The reactor's heating fouls until its valve saturates TIC-301 lost control (or R-301) reactor_sensor_bias TT-301 reads high; the loop cools the true temperature to match a measurement fault on TT-301 reactor_sensor_drift TT-301 drifts high a measurement fault on TT-301 catalyst_loss The catalyst loses activity; nothing measured moves an unmeasured change in R-301

A process hypothesis claims that its tag moved and caused the deviation, so it counts only when the tag itself is listed: a tag that merely sits on the faulty equipment does not. The other kinds (a setpoint change, lost control, a measurement fault, an unmeasured change) are claims about their node.

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
Metric Definition Release gate hit@3 Share of scenarios where one of the top three hypotheses names the cause ≥ 70% on the hidden split hit@1 The same for the leading hypothesis reported Wrong-confident rate Share of scenarios where the leading hypothesis is labeled high confidence and is wrong < 10% Data-fault catch rate Among measurement faults, share where the faulty tag leads as a measurement fault ≥ 90%

Rates carry a 95% Wilson interval in bench.json: at 85 scenarios an observed 96% is anything from 90% to 99%.

items.title: Splits and calibration
items.text:
Split Seed Used for train public (1000) Fitting the test weights and rule scores validation public (2000) Choosing the confidence thresholds, and the numbers above hidden KausalFlow's secret The release gate, run by hand before a release (the Release gate workflow)

scripts/fit_calibration.py searches the weights and rule scores on the train split (maximizing hit@3, plus half of hit@1 and half of the data-fault catch rate), then chooses the confidence thresholds on validation so that the wrong-confident rate stays at or under 5%. The result ships as src/penguineer/engines/calibration.json, and every report.json names the splits and the Homeostat version it was fitted with.

items.title: What the numbers do not say
items.text:
• The bench is one plant family. A real plant has more tags, more loops and other faults, so treat these numbers as an upper bound, not a promise.
  • The data-fault catch rate is 95% (19 of 20) on validation and 100% (21 of 21) on train, but 20 scenarios give a wide interval: 76% to 99%. The one miss is a small bias that started seven hours before the first off-spec lot, inside the newest reference lot (the lots in between ran another grade), so the loop output's move is partly in the reference and the leading hypothesis is an unmeasured change in R-301.
  • The plant has no analyzer on the sampled stream, so the onset test never runs on the bench, and its weight is kept rather than fitted.
  • The hidden split, and so the release gate, is not run by the public bench. The Release gate workflow runs it by hand before a release, with the seed from a repository secret, and shows only the summary scores (python -m penguineer.bench.gate bench.json); the plants and per-scenario results never leave the runner. The gate also needs at least 150 scenarios and no errors.

items.title: In CI
items.text: The Bench workflow runs a smoke bench (3 validation plants per fault type) on every pull request, and the full train and validation bench every night. Each run uploads bench.json and scenarios.csv and writes the scores into the job summary.

items.title: One definition per command
items.text:
A command is four things registered under a name: a Pydantic Params model, a Pydantic Result model, a run(params, ctx) function and its docstring as help text.

class DataHealthParams(CommandParams):
    data: FilePath = Field(description="Historian export, CSV or Parquet, wide or long")
    graph: FilePath | None = Field(None, description="Plant graph")
    spike_z: float = Field(8.0, gt=0, description="Robust z-score on first differences")


@command("data health", params=DataHealthParams, result=DataHealthResult)
def data_health(p: DataHealthParams, ctx: RunContext) -> DataHealthResult:
    """Flag frozen tags, gaps, spikes, out-of-range values and timestamp problems."""

From that one definition penguineer generates:

  • the Typer command penguineer data health, with one option per field, its type, default and help, and file options that must exist;
  • the --json output, which is the Result model;
  • the Python call penguineer.run("data health", data=...), which returns the same Result;
  • the JSON Schemas in penguineer.schemas(), which Alchemist builds its agent tools and forms from.

Pydantic validates the parsed values, so the CLI and the Python API report the same errors. A group name such as data in data health comes from the registered name.

items.title: The equivalent command line
items.text: to_argv(command, params) turns validated params into the canonical command line, leaving out defaults. A property test generates random params and checks that the CLI parses to_argv(params) back to the same params. This is what makes "the command this run equals" in a run record true.

items.title: Run context
items.text: RunContext carries the project folder, the run ID, a seeded random generator, the LLM mode, the cache folder, a progress callback and a cancellation flag. Engines read only this context and never global state. All outputs of a call go under its project folder, so several penguineer processes can run side by side on different folders. Alchemist relies on this to run one call per runner.

items.title: Run records
items.text: Every call, from the CLI or Python, writes runs/<run_id>/run.json, also when it fails. See Run record for its fields.

items.title: Exit codes
items.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Validation failed, for example errors in graph check 2 Usage error: bad options or missing files 3 Not enough data to answer 4 Internal error, or the command is not implemented yet

items.title: Data health
items.text:
penguineer data health says whether the data can be trusted before anyone blames the process. Each check writes findings: intervals on one tag with a severity (info, warning or critical), a plain-language detail and the numbers behind it.

Check Method Severity gap An interval between samples longer than --gap-factor (3) times the tag's median period warning; critical beyond 60 times flatline Consecutive values that change by at most --deadband for at least --flatline-minutes (60) warning; critical beyond 24 h out_of_range Values outside the instrument range of the tag node in the graph critical spike A robust z-score on first differences above --spike-z (8), where the signal returns to its level within a few samples. A level shift is a process change, not a spike, and is not reported warning timestamp Duplicate timestamps, irregular sampling, and local times that do not exist (the daylight-saving change) warning or info

Setpoints, modes and settings (from the tag's role, or a loop's sp and mode) are never reported as frozen. Without --graph, the out-of-range check is skipped and the result says so.

Checks that compare an online analyzer with lab results (drifting bias, calibration steps, clock offset) need LIMS input and come later. The result lists them under checks_not_run.

items.title: Output
items.text:
health.json holds the result without its own path, so the same inputs and options give a byte-identical file. It is written to the run folder unless --out says otherwise. It also has a per-tag summary: sample count, first and last time, median period, coverage (the share of expected samples present), the number of findings and the worst severity.

Health findings are evidence in their own right. In investigate, a faulty tag on a causal path will become a hypothesis of the kind "the measurement is wrong", competing with process causes.

items.title: Dead times
items.text: Material takes time to travel through a plant. A change in the feed shows up in the reactor minutes later and in the product sample hours later. penguineer keeps these delays on the flows_to edges of the plant graph (dead_time_min, with dead_time_low_min and dead_time_high_min as its interval), and investigate will use them to line up each cause with the quality it affects.

items.title: Estimating them from data
items.text:
uv run penguineer graph lags --data historian.csv --graph graph.yaml

For every flows_to edge whose two ends are each measured by a tag (through a measures edge), graph lags estimates how long the downstream signal lags the upstream one:

  1. Both tags are resampled to one grid, by default the slower tag's median sample period (--step-seconds overrides it).
  2. An AR model is fitted to the upstream signal, with its order chosen by AIC, and both series are filtered with it. This is prewhitening: process signals are so autocorrelated that a raw cross-correlation has a broad hump instead of a peak.
  3. The cross-correlation of the filtered series is computed for every lag up to --max-lag-minutes (240). The dead time is the lag with the largest absolute correlation. A negative correlation means a reverse-acting link.
  4. The interval is the run of lags around the peak whose correlation is within the noise band (2/√n) of it.
  5. The estimate is kept only when the peak is strong enough: |corr|·√n at least --z-threshold (5).
Edge status Meaning estimated A clear lag was found and written to the edge as inferred, with source data and the correlation as its confidence no_clear_lag Both ends are measured but no lag stands out of the noise kept_confirmed An engineer confirmed this edge, so it is never overwritten no_tags One end has no measuring tag no_data The tags are not in the export, or overlap too little

items.title: Where the result goes
items.text: By default the updated graph is written to the run folder (runs/<run_id>/graph.yaml), and the input graph is not touched. With --in-place, the estimates are written back into --graph, and each change is appended to graph.history.jsonl next to it, with the time, the run ID, the reason and the edge before and after.

items.title: Limits
items.text: The estimate is a transport delay between two measured points, from the data as it is. Feedback control, recycles and mixing all smear a delay. Mixing in a vessel spreads a step out over its residence time, so the peak marks where the response is strongest, not where it starts. investigate aligns in material time, which accounts for flow-dependent delays. To read how a delay depends on the flow, and how much mixing spreads it, use penguineer lag on the two tags.

items.title: Investigating an off-spec lot
items.text:
investigate takes one lot, finds the lab result that was out of spec, and ranks the process variables that could have caused it. Every hypothesis comes with its tests, its path through the plant graph, and plots. The engines are deterministic Python; an LLM can write the summary at the top of the report (see Using an LLM), and never touches the ranking.

uv run penguineer investigate --lot L0803-A \
  --lims examples/offspec/lims.csv --data examples/offspec/historian.csv \
  --graph examples/offspec/graph.yaml --lots examples/offspec/lots.csv

investigate: lot L0803-A, purity 98.2 wt% (spec >= 99), sampled 2026-08-03 07:59 at SP-1

  #1 TI-101.PV  high   score 0.97  process
     TI-101.PV (E-101) ran 5.74 degC low from 2026-08-03 05:29, 50 min upstream of the sample point; purity moved when it arrived.
  #2 PT-100.PV  medium score 0.46  process
     PT-100.PV (S-feed) ran 1.02 bar low from 2026-08-03 05:27, 52 min upstream of the sample point; purity moved 55 min after the expected arrival.
  #3 PI-103.PV  medium score 0.45  measurement_fault
     PI-103.PV has a flatline finding in the lot window: value frozen at 5.968 for 90 min

ruled out:
  FI-102.PV: held at setpoint by FIC-102 while its output moved 9.1 (+34.0 reference scales)
  TI-104.PV: its shift of -2.88 is 100% predicted from TI-101.PV (regression on the reference lots)
  PI-103.PV: did not move in the lot

The demo plant in examples/offspec/ has a known answer: the feed preheater E-101 fouls, its outlet temperature TI-101 falls 6 °C, and the product purity follows 50 minutes later. A feed pressure dip at nearly the same time is a decoy, because the flow loop absorbs it. scripts/make_offspec_demo.py writes the data and documents every injected event.

Open the example report: report.html, as investigate writes it.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
1. Resolve. Find the lot's results in the LIMS export, keep the properties that have a Quality node in the graph, and pick the one furthest out of spec (--quality picks one). Follow reported_as and samples edges to the node where the sample is taken. The lot window comes from --lots (a CSV of lot, start, end), or else runs from the previous lab sample of the same property to this one.
  2. Candidates. Walk flows_to edges upstream from the sampled node (--hops, 6). Every measurement tag on those nodes is a candidate. Tags on the sampled node itself, such as an online analyzer, are symptoms, not causes: the first one is used to time the quality change.
  3. Regime, onset and reference. Mode tags (role: mode in the graph, such as a grade) label the operating regime. The quality is assumed to have started moving in the lot before this one, or earlier when the lab results of the same regime step before the first off-spec lot (lots already affected but still in spec). The reference is the most recent in-spec lots of the same regime that end before that (--reference-lots, 3), so it is not made of material the fault had already reached. Without one, the command exits with code 3, because there is nothing to compare with.
  4. Align. All series go on one grid (the slowest candidate's period, or --step-seconds) in material time at the sampled node: a tag with a cumulative dead time D along its path is read at t − D. Gaps longer than five sample periods stay empty rather than being interpolated across.
  5. Test. Each candidate gets three tests (below), each with a strength from 0 to 1, and a score from them. Without an online analyzer on the sampled stream there is no quality onset to time against, so the effect is measured from the candidate's own step when it lands where the quality moved, and the correlation test uses earlier lab results instead of the analyzer.
  6. Loop check. For a tag that is a loop's process value: if the setpoint moved, the setpoint change becomes its own hypothesis (an operator or recipe action). If the output saturated while the process value deviated, the hypothesis becomes lost control. If the process value held while the output moved, the loop absorbed a disturbance: the process value is ruled out and the output move is attached as evidence to the candidates upstream of the loop that moved and whose shift predicts at least 30% of the output's move (a regression on the reference lots: a tag the output never followed does not explain it). Held means the process value did not move by two reference scales, or that, once the loop had 20 minutes to settle after its output stepped, the median control error sits within the process value's sample noise of the reference's: a controlled value barely moves from lot to lot, so the short spike while the loop recovers would otherwise pass for a large move. When no upstream candidate explains the output, two hypotheses take their place: the process value reads wrong (a biased transmitter makes the loop hold the true value away from its setpoint), and something unmeasured disturbed the loop.
  7. Explain away. When an upstream and a downstream candidate both moved, a regression on the reference lots predicts the downstream shift from the upstream one. If it explains at least 60% of it, the downstream tag is demoted and recorded as explained away.
  8. Hidden change. When no measured tag moved clearly, the quality still moved: "something unmeasured changed just upstream of the sample" (a catalyst, a fouled surface, a feed component nobody analyzes) becomes a hypothesis at the nearest equipment.
  9. Data faults. A candidate tag with a health finding (gap, flatline, spike, out of range) in its window also becomes a measurement-fault hypothesis, so a wrong measurement competes with the process causes.
  10. Rank and label. Hypotheses are sorted by score. The leading one is labeled high confidence when its score and its lead over the next pass the calibrated thresholds; others are medium above a lower one. The weights and rule scores are fitted on the public homeostat training split and the thresholds on its validation split (see The homeostat bench); report.json records the values used.

items.title: The tests
items.text:
Test What it asks Strength Effect size Did the tag sit away from its reference level while the quality was off? Measured on a 30-minute moving mean, in units of the reference's spread or of the tag's lot-to-lot spread over earlier lots, whichever is larger, so a tag that wanders slowly does not count as moved 0 below 2 scales, 1 from 6 Onset Does the tag's step, shifted by its dead time, land on the moment the quality moved? 1 on time, falling off over the dead-time interval (at least 10 min); 0 when the tag moved after the quality Lag correlation Over the reference lots, does the shifted tag track the quality, with a sign that fits this deviation? |r|, or 0 when the sign does not fit

The score is their weighted mean (fitted weights; 0.5, 0.3 and 0.3 at present), halved when the tag did not move at all, and halved again when the tag has a data health finding in the window.

items.title: The report
items.text:
Each run writes reports/<run_id>/ in the project (or --out):

File Contents report.json The Report model: the quality event, regime, reference lots, ranked hypotheses with their tests, ruled-out candidates, evidence items, health findings, notes and the summary report.html One self-contained page rendered from report.json, with images from evidence/ report.md The same in Markdown llm-request.json With --llm-dry-run only: what would have been sent to the LLM evidence/ quality.png (the quality over the period with the lot and reference windows) and one trend per hypothesis, shifted into material time

The command's --json output carries the event, the hypotheses and the ruled-out list, so a caller does not need to read the files.

items.title: Not yet
items.text: Change points on key flows as regime boundaries, flow-dependent dead times (penguineer lag) inside the ranking, the valve stiction test and PLS contribution analysis come later.

items.title: Finding the actual lag
items.text:
The dead times on the plant graph are often a guess: a volume over a design flow, or an engineer's memory. penguineer lag reads the actual delay from the data, between two tags or from a tag to a lab result, and says how the material travels: with a fixed delay, a delay that follows the flow, or a delay with mixing.

penguineer lag --data historian.parquet --cause FT-102 \
  --effect product_property --lims lims.csv --flow FT-101 --flow FT-102 \
  --max-lag-minutes 150

lag: FT-102 -> product_property (lab, 476 lab samples)
flow: FT-101 + FT-102, mean 20.1 m3/h

  model   dead                      mixing                delay   corr  strength
  fixed   34.54 min [20.17, 46.64]  -                 34.54 min  +0.67  3.86x chance
  flow    10.14 m3 [7.182, 14.36]   -                 30.25 min  +0.68  3.93x chance
  mixing  7.943 m3 [0, 13.52]       4.442 m3 [0, 17]  36.95 min  +0.70  4.06x chance

best: plug flow through 7.943 m3, then a mixed volume of 4.442 m3: 36.95 min on average at the mean flow
plot: runs/<run_id>/lag-profile.png
plot: runs/<run_id>/lag-fit.png

The run folder gets two plots: lag-profile.png, each model's correlation over the delay it tries, and lag-fit.png, the effect with the cause moved by each fitted model.

items.title: Three ways material travels
items.text:
Model Parameters The delay is Right when fixed a dead time constant the throughput is steady flow a dead volume the volume over the throughput, so it changes with the flow material moves in plug flow, as in a pipe mixing a dead volume and a mixed volume plug flow, then a first-order spread whose time constant is the mixed volume over the throughput the line has a stirred vessel, or back-mixing

The flow and mixing models count the delay in volume instead of time ("material time"): the cumulative throughput of the --flow tags, summed. A change at the cause reaches the effect when the dead volume has flowed past, however long that takes. Volumes are in the flow tag's unit times hours (m3 for a flow in m3/h; --flow-unit names it). Without --flow, the mixing model works in time instead: a dead time, then a time constant.

The delay column is each model's mean delay in minutes at the mean flow: the dead part plus the mixing part, which is the number to compare with a dead time on the plant graph.

items.title: How the delay is found
items.text:
1. The cause and the flows are resampled to an even grid, by default the cause's median sample period.
  2. Each model tries every delay up to --max-lag-minutes (240), and the mixing model a range of mixed volumes for each: the cause is spread by the mixing, shifted by the dead part, and read at the effect's times.
  3. The prediction is compared with the effect by correlation:
    • An online effect is compared on the grid after prewhitening both with one AR model of the cause, as in graph lags, so that slow drifts do not pass for a link. A peak counts when |corr|·√n reaches --z-threshold (5).
    • A lab effect is compared at its sample times. The chance level comes from running the same search on the cause rotated by a random offset, 59 times per model: rotation cuts the link but keeps the cause's own slow swings. A peak counts when it beats every rotated search of every model (the strength column is the ratio).
  4. A coarse scan finds the peak, and a finer one around it gives the estimate. The interval is the run of values whose |corr| is within two standard errors of the peak's.
  5. The result names the fixed or the flow model, whichever correlates more, unless the mixing model's extra parameter explains significantly more of the effect (an F test on r², p ≈ 0.01).

items.title: Checked on Homeostat plants
items.text:
scripts/validate_lag.py runs the bench plant with no fault and no grade change, its feed flows swinging ±10% within the hour, and the reactor's back-mixing drawn per plant, so the true volumes are known. It fits feed B's flow (FT-102) against the lab's product property, with the total flow FT-101 + FT-102: the change crosses the mixer's outlet pipe and the reactor in plug flow, then the reactor's back-mixing spreads it.

With a lab result every hour over 20 days (about 480 results), on six plants:

Plant True dead True mixed True delay Fitted dead Fitted mixed Fitted delay Fixed model Chosen 0 8.46 m3 5.80 m3 43.3 min 8.22 m3 4.97 m3 40.1 min 29.1 min fixed 1 5.92 m3 2.52 m3 25.3 min 5.96 m3 1.74 m3 23.1 min 23.4 min mixing 2 8.26 m3 4.51 m3 38.1 min 7.94 m3 4.44 m3 37.0 min 34.5 min mixing 3 7.03 m3 2.01 m3 27.5 min 7.53 m3 1.44 m3 27.3 min 28.5 min flow 4 5.66 m3 2.62 m3 25.1 min 5.66 m3 2.96 m3 26.1 min 25.6 min mixing 5 6.60 m3 2.11 m3 25.8 min 6.99 m3 2.47 m3 28.0 min 25.8 min mixing

The mixing model finds the dead volume within 0.25 m3 on average and the mixed volume within 0.5 m3, and the mean delay within 1.7 minutes; the fixed model's delay is off by 3.5 minutes on average, and by 14 minutes on plant 0, the plant with the most mixing, where the noisier data leave the choice at the fixed model. The intervals are wide (the dead volume's often starts at 0), because a dead volume and a mixed volume trade off against each other when the data are sparse. The example at the top of this page is plant 2.

With the usual lab rhythm, a result every 4 hours, 60 days give about 360 results. The mixing model is chosen on five of the six plants, and its mean delay is off by 2.1 minutes on average (dead volume 0.9 m3, mixed volume 1.1 m3); the fixed model's by 4.3 minutes. Three days of 4-hourly results (18 of them) are too few: under 20 results the command stops with exit code 3. A lag from lab data needs weeks.

The script also fits FT-102 against the online analyzer AT-101 on the mixer's outlet. There the analyzer's own reporting delay and sample hold (about 11 minutes, at any flow) blur the transport, and the models agree within about 2 minutes of the true mean delay.

uv sync --extra bench
uv run python scripts/validate_lag.py --plants 6 --days 20 --lab-hours 1
uv run python scripts/validate_lag.py --plants 6 --days 60 --lab-hours 4

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• A lag can only be read where the cause moves. A tag held still by a controller, or a feed that never changes, carries no delay to find, and the result says no model is above chance.
  • Lab results are sparse: weeks of them are needed, and the chance level is honest about it. Grade changes and other large steps dominate a correlation of levels, so pick a window of steady operation with --start and --end.
  • The models are for transport. A link through a controller, a recycle or a heat balance has a delay too, but it is not a volume, and the mixing model may fit it with a misleading one.
  • Several causes moving together share their delays: the fit finds the delay of whatever moves the effect, which need not be the tag named.

items.title: The plant graph
items.text:
The plant context graph lives in its own small package, plantgraph, which depends only on Pydantic. penguineer and homeostat both import it, so a real plant and a simulated one are described by the same types.

Every node and edge carries a stable id, a provenance (declared, inferred or confirmed), a source (user, llm, data, dexpi or homeostat), a confidence between 0 and 1, and valid_from and valid_to dates. graph.valid_on(day) gives the plant as it was on that day.

items.title: Nodes
items.text:
Type What it represents Key fields unit The scope of one project name equipment Vessels, exchangers, columns, pumps kind, holdup_m3 stream A material flow between equipment phase tag One historian signal tag, unit_of_measure, range_low, range_high, role loop A control loop pv, sp, op, mode (IDs of tag nodes) actuator A valve or drive a loop moves kind sample_point Where a lab sample is taken quality A LIMS property with a spec property, spec_low, spec_high

A tag's role is measurement, setpoint, output, mode or setting. Setpoints, modes and settings may sit still for days, so data health never reports them as frozen.

items.title: Edges
items.text: Type From → to Key fields flows_to equipment or stream → equipment or stream dead_time_min with an interval, recycle measures tag → equipment or stream measured_variable controls loop → actuator acting manipulates actuator → equipment or stream samples sample point → equipment or stream reported_as sample point → quality affects any → any a cause link an engineer asserts

items.title: In YAML
items.text:
schema_version: 1
unit: demo-reactor
nodes:
  - {id: R-101, type: equipment, kind: vessel, holdup_m3: 12.0}
  - {id: TI-101, type: tag, tag: TI-101.PV, unit_of_measure: degC, range_low: 0, range_high: 300}
edges:
  - {id: m1, type: measures, from: TI-101, to: R-101, measured_variable: temperature}

items.title: Checking a graph
items.text: penguineer graph check --graph graph.yaml validates the schema and these plant rules: unique IDs, no edges to unknown nodes, edge endpoints of the right types, every loop with a PV and an OP, flows_to cycles only through an edge flagged as recycle, and every quality reachable from a sample point on the plant. It then lists the confirm queue: inferred edges, sorted by how many qualities depend on them. It exits with 1 when there are errors.

items.title: Drafting a graph from a tag list
items.text:
penguineer graph draft writes a first graph.yaml from the historian's tag list, so that an engineer starts by confirming a draft rather than typing every node.

penguineer graph draft --tags tags.csv
penguineer graph check --graph graph.yaml

The tag list is a CSV with a tag column and, if the export has them, description, unit, equipment, range_low and range_high (common alternatives such as TagName, UOM or Max are recognized).

graph draft: 14 tags, 2 loops, 2 valves, 2 equipment; 5 edges (0 flows_to), all inferred
wrote graph.yaml
1 tags without an ISA-5.1 name: GRADE
warning: TT-305: the name says temperature but the unit 'bar' is a pressure
note: no piping (flows_to) in a tag list: add it, give the P&ID with --pid, or confirm what the LLM proposes
next: penguineer graph check --graph graph.yaml

The draft reads each name with ISA-5.1 conventions:

Part Example Read as First letter FIC-102, TT-301, PDI-5 The measured variable: flow, temperature, pressure, level (L), analysis (A), ... Modifier PDI-5, FQI-7 Differential, totalized or ratio Function letters FIC-102, FT-102, FV-102 Controller, transmitter, indicator, valve, ... Number FIC-102 The loop: FIC-102, FT-102 and FV-102 belong together Prefix 11FIC1001, U1.TI101 A plant or area code, kept as part of the loop Suffix FIC-102.SP, TIC-301.out The signal: PV, SP, OP (or OUT, MV), MODE

From that it drafts:

  • a tag node for every tag, with its role (measurement, setpoint, output, mode);
  • a loop for every group with a controller (letter C) or a setpoint or output signal: its PV is the controller's own measurement, else the group's transmitter or indicator;
  • the actuator each loop drives, from the group's valve tag (FV-102) or named by convention, with a controls edge;
  • equipment from the equipment column, or from equipment IDs in the descriptions ("Reactor R-101 temperature" gives R-101, a reactor), with a measures edge from the tag.

Every drafted node and edge is inferred, with a confidence (lower when it comes from a description or a naming convention than from a column or a tag in the list), so all of them appear in graph check's confirm queue. A unit that contradicts the name is reported. Tags without an ISA-5.1 name, such as GRADE, become tag nodes without a role.

A tag list does not say how material flows, so on its own the draft has no flows_to edges and no streams. Sample points and qualities come from the engineer.

items.title: Adding the P&ID
items.text:
With a DEXPI P&ID (the Proteus XML that P&ID tools export), the draft also reads how the plant is piped and where its instruments sit:

penguineer graph draft --tags tags.csv --pid pid.xml

graph draft: 13 tags, 2 loops, 2 valves, 3 equipment; 19 edges (9 flows_to), all inferred
wrote graph.yaml
1 tags without an ISA-5.1 name: GRADE
warning: P&ID instrument PI-305 has no tag in the tag list
next: penguineer graph check --graph graph.yaml

From the P&ID it drafts:

  • equipment for every piece of equipment, by its tag name, with its kind from the DEXPI class (TubularHeatExchanger is an exchanger);
  • a stream for every off-page connector: a feed where material comes in, a product where it leaves;
  • a flows_to edge wherever a pipe runs from one piece of equipment (or a feed) to the next, through tees, reducers and valves, in the direction the P&ID draws its connections;
  • for each instrument function that matches the tag list by letter and number (TIC-201 on the P&ID is TIC-201.SP, TT-201 and the rest in the list; a plant prefix is ignored): a measures edge from its sensor's tag to where the sensor sits, and, for a controller, the valve its signal goes to as the loop's actuator, with a manipulates edge to the equipment that valve's pipe feeds.

A sensor on a nozzle measures that equipment (confidence 0.85). A sensor on a pipe is read as measuring the equipment the pipe comes from, and a valve on a pipe as acting on the equipment it goes to (0.6): confirm those. When the tag list says otherwise and is more sure (its equipment column, or a valve tag in the list), the tag list's answer is kept and the difference is reported. Instruments on the P&ID without a tag in the list are reported too. Everything from the P&ID has source: dexpi and is inferred, like the rest of the draft.

items.title: Asking an LLM for the rest
items.text:
What the rules and the P&ID leave open, an LLM can propose: which equipment a tag measures when its description names none, what a valve acts on, and, without a P&ID, the piping.

penguineer graph draft --tags tags.csv --llm local --llm-model <model>

graph draft: 7 tags, 1 loops, 1 valves, 2 equipment; 6 edges (1 flows_to), all inferred
wrote graph.yaml
1 tags without an ISA-5.1 name: GRADE
note: the LLM proposed 4 relations; 3 kept (source llm), 1 rejected
note: rejected LLM proposal R-101 -flows_to-> E-201: would close a cycle
next: penguineer graph check --graph graph.yaml

The LLM sees the plant's equipment, streams and valves, the relations already drafted, and the open tags with their names, units and descriptions; never any data. It may only link nodes that exist. A proposal is kept only if both ends have the right types, it places a tag or valve that was open (it never changes a drafted relation), it does not repeat an edge, and its piping closes no cycle; the summary lists every rejected one and why. Kept edges have source: llm, are inferred, and get a confidence of 0.3 to 0.5, below every rule-based edge. --llm-dry-run writes the requests to llm-request.json next to the graph and sends nothing. See Using an LLM for choosing a model.

items.title: Homeostat Live
items.text: Homeostat Live publishes a simulated plant's sensor data every 10 minutes, its released lab results and its data dictionary. The first plant is isidis-01, a Sabatier methane plant whose lab reports methane purity.

items.title: Download a week
items.text:
uv run python scripts/fetch_homeostat_live.py --plant isidis-01 \
  --since 2026-10-02T17:00:00+00:00 --until 2026-10-09T17:00:00+00:00 \
  --out data/isidis-01

This writes four files into data/isidis-01/:

File What live.csv Sensor rows, a wide historian export with a time column, fetched in 7-day chunks because the API answers at most 1,100 rows at a time lab.csv Lab results: tag, name, unit, sampled_at, reported_at, value tags.csv The data dictionary graph.yaml A plant graph derived from the dictionary

Files that are already there are reused, so a released week is downloaded once.

items.title: The derived graph
items.text: penguineer.io.homeostat_live.graph_from_tags builds a graph from the public dictionary: a tag node per sensor with its unit, its role and its instrument range (parsed from text such as "gas flow transmitter, 0-20 Nm3/h"), a loop per control group that has an output, and a quality node per lab analysis. The flow topology is not in the public dictionary, so the graph has no edges yet.

items.title: Check the data
items.text: uv run penguineer data health --data data/isidis-01/live.csv --graph data/isidis-01/graph.yaml

items.title: In the tests
items.text: tests/test_homeostat_live.py runs on the plant's first public benchmark week, 2 to 9 October 2026. That week is released and frozen, so its data never changes. The tests are skipped without network access. CI sets PENGUINEER_REQUIRE_HOMEOSTAT=1, so there they fail instead of skipping. Downloads are cached in PENGUINEER_HOMEOSTAT_CACHE, by default tests/.cache/homeostat/.

items.title: Using an LLM
items.text:
Two commands can use an LLM, and both check what it returns before using it:

  • investigate can have it write the summary at the top of its report. The LLM only writes prose: the hypotheses, their ranking, scores and confidence labels are the same with or without it.
  • graph draft can have it propose the relations its rules could not infer, as inferred edges for the engineer to confirm (Asking an LLM for the rest).

Without --llm, or with --llm none (the default), penguineer makes no network call: the summary comes from a template and the graph draft from the rules.

penguineer investigate --lot L0803-A --lims lims.csv --data historian.parquet \
  --llm local --llm-model <model>

items.title: Choose a model
items.text:
--llm Where it goes Needs none Nowhere: the template summary Nothing local Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint on the machine or the plant network: Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM llm.base_url (default http://localhost:11434/v1, Ollama's) api Anthropic's or OpenAI's API pip install "penguineer[llm-api]" and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY

penguineer has no default model: which model may read a plant's results is the plant's decision. Name it with --llm-model, PENGUINEER_LLM_MODEL, or in penguineer.yaml:

llm:
  mode: local
  model: <model>                        # as the endpoint names it
  base_url: http://localhost:11434/v1   # local only
  provider: anthropic                   # api only: anthropic or openai

--llm and --llm-model override the environment (PENGUINEER_LLM_MODEL, PENGUINEER_LLM_BASE_URL, PENGUINEER_LLM_PROVIDER), which overrides the file. A local endpoint that needs a key reads it from PENGUINEER_LLM_API_KEY.

items.title: What leaves the machine
items.text:
For graph draft, the LLM receives the plant's equipment, streams and valves, the relations already drafted, and the open tags' names, units and descriptions. For investigate, it receives the results of report.json, never the historian or LIMS data: the quality event, the reference lots' lab values, the hypotheses with their tests and evidence IDs, the evidence titles, the ruled-out candidates and the notes. --llm-dry-run writes the exact request to llm-request.json in the report folder and prints it, without sending anything, so it can be shown to OT security first:

penguineer investigate --lot L0803-A --lims lims.csv --data historian.parquet \
  --llm api --llm-model <model> --llm-dry-run

A dry run needs neither the SDK nor a key.

items.title: How the summary is checked
items.text:
The LLM answers in a fixed structure: an overview, and up to three claims, each naming one hypothesis's cause, a confidence and the evidence IDs behind it. penguineer keeps the answer only if

  • every claim names a hypothesis's cause, with a confidence no higher than its label;
  • every claim cites at least one evidence ID, and every cited ID exists in the report;
  • no sentence names a tag or node of the plant graph that the hypotheses, their paths and the ruled-out list do not mention;
  • no sentence states a higher confidence than the label allows, or calls anything certain, proven or definite.

Otherwise the report shows the template summary and says why the LLM's was not used, as it does when the endpoint cannot be reached. The report names the provider, the model and the prompt version of a summary it kept.

items.title: Reproducibility
items.text: Prompts are versioned files in the package (penguineer/llm/prompts/summary-1.md, relations-1.md). Answers are cached in .penguineer/cache/llm/ by a hash of the prompt version, the provider, the model and the request, so re-running a report on the same results gives the same text without a second call. The run record stores the provider, the model and the prompts used (llm_provider, llm_model, llm_prompts).

items.title: MCP server
items.text:
penguineer mcp serves every command as a tool to an MCP client, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop or an IDE assistant. The assistant can then check a graph, look at data health, fit a lag or investigate a lot by itself, and read the same results you get from --json.

pip install "penguineer[mcp]"

The server talks over stdin and stdout to the client that starts it. It opens no port and has no web UI.

items.title: Add it to a client
items.text:
Claude Code:

claude mcp add penguineer -- penguineer mcp --project /path/to/my-unit

A client configured with a JSON file (Claude Desktop, and most others):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "penguineer": {
      "command": "penguineer",
      "args": ["mcp", "--project", "/path/to/my-unit"]
    }
  }
}

--project is the default project folder. Each call writes its outputs and its run record under it, as the CLI does, and relative paths in a call are read against it. A call can name another folder with its own project argument.

items.title: The tools
items.text:
One tool per command, named after it with underscores:

Tool Command init penguineer init data_health penguineer data health graph_check penguineer graph check graph_draft penguineer graph draft graph_lags penguineer graph lags lag penguineer lag investigate penguineer investigate bench_homeostat penguineer bench homeostat (needs penguineer[bench] too)

Each tool's input schema is the command's parameters, the same as in the CLI reference, plus project and seed. Its output schema is the command's result. A call returns the result as structured content, and the CLI summary with the path of the run record as text:

graph check: 13 nodes, 11 edges, 0 errors, 0 warnings
confirm queue (1 inferred edges):
  f3: R-101 -flows_to-> S-product (confidence 0.60, 1 qualities depend on it)
run record: /path/to/my-unit/runs/20261018T001610Z-b414d1/run.json

{
  "graph": "/path/to/my-unit/graph.yaml",
  "n_nodes": 13,
  "n_edges": 11,
  "errors": 0,
  "warnings": 0,
  "issues": [],
  "confirm_queue": [
    {"edge_id": "f3", "type": "flows_to", "from_id": "R-101", "to_id": "S-product",
     "confidence": 0.6, "dependent_qualities": 1}
  ]
}

A failed call returns an error with the CLI's exit code and message, for example graph check failed (exit code 2): ... for a missing file. Commands that report progress (graph lags, investigate, bench homeostat) send it as MCP progress notifications when the client asks for them.

items.title: How it runs
items.text:
• One call at a time, like the CLI: a second call waits for the first to finish.
  • The engines are the same deterministic code as the CLI. The server adds no LLM, and the assistant only sees what the tools return.
  • Tools write only under the project folder, except graph lags --in-place, which writes back to the graph you name, and an --out folder you name.

items.title: Python API
items.text:
The Python API mirrors the CLI one to one.

import penguineer

result = penguineer.run(
    "data health",
    data="data/isidis-01/live.csv",
    graph="data/isidis-01/graph.yaml",
    project="my-unit",
)
for finding in result.findings:
    print(finding.severity, finding.tag, finding.detail)

penguineer.run(name, **params) validates the params, runs the command and returns its Result model. You can pass a Params object instead of keyword arguments. Invalid params raise UsageError. Other failures raise subclasses of PenguineerError, each carrying the CLI's exit_code.

penguineer.execute(...) takes the same arguments plus progress and cancelled callbacks and a cache_dir. It returns a RunOutcome with the result, the record (the run record) and the run_dir.

penguineer.schemas() returns the JSON Schema of every command's Params and Result, keyed by command name.

items.title: For Alchemist
items.text:
Alchemist lists penguineer as a dependency and imports it. A thin wrapper inside Alchemist turns commands into agent tools from penguineer.schemas(), passes staged Parquet snapshots as the file params, maps progress and cancelled to its step progress and steering, and copies run.json and the outputs into its run folder before sealing. penguineer never imports Alchemist.

The Params and Result schemas are frozen by a snapshot test (tests/snapshots/schemas.json), so a change that would break Alchemist shows up in review. penguineer follows semantic versioning from v0.1.

items.title: CLI reference
items.text:
Every command also takes --json (print the result model as JSON on stdout), --project PATH (the folder run records and outputs go under, default .) and --seed INT (default 0).

Exit codes: 0 success, 1 validation failed, 2 usage error, 3 not enough data, 4 internal error or not implemented yet.

items.title: penguineer bench homeostat
items.text:
Run investigate on homeostat plants with injected faults and score it.

Option Type Default Description --scenarios train | validation | hidden validation Which scenario split to run --bundles existing folder Folder of exported scenario bundles (default: generate them with Homeostat into .penguineer/bench/ in the project) --per-fault int 12 Plants per fault type to generate --faults str, repeatable Fault types to generate (default: all) --split-seed int Seed of the split (train and validation have fixed public seeds; the hidden split needs its secret one) --limit int Run at most this many scenarios --out path Folder for bench.json and scenarios.csv (default: the run folder)

items.title: penguineer data health
items.text:
Flag frozen tags, gaps, spikes, out-of-range values and timestamp problems.

Option Type Default Description --data existing file required Historian export, CSV or Parquet, wide or long --graph existing file Plant graph; instrument ranges and loop setpoints come from it --start datetime Window start (inclusive) --end datetime Window end (exclusive) --tags str, repeatable Only check these tags --timezone str UTC Time zone of naive timestamps in the export --gap-factor float 3.0 Gap when an interval exceeds this × median --flatline-minutes float 60.0 Shortest frozen run to report --deadband float 0.0 Changes up to this count as frozen --spike-z float 8.0 Robust z-score on first differences --out path Where to write health.json (default: run folder)

items.title: penguineer graph check
items.text:
Validate the plant graph and list inferred edges to confirm, most important first.

Option Type Default Description --graph existing file required Plant graph in the plantgraph schema

items.title: penguineer graph draft
items.text:
Draft the plant graph from a tag list and an optional P&ID; every edge is inferred.

Option Type Default Description --tags existing file required Tag list as CSV: tag, and optionally description, unit, equipment, range_low, range_high --pid existing file DEXPI P&ID (Proteus XML): equipment, piping, where sensors and valves sit --out path graph.yaml Where to write the drafted graph (relative: the project) --unit str Unit name (default: the project folder's name) --force bool False Overwrite an existing graph --llm none | local | api none LLM for relations rules cannot infer --llm-model str Model for --llm (default: llm.model in penguineer.yaml) --llm-dry-run bool False Write what would be sent to the LLM, and send nothing

items.title: penguineer graph lags
items.text:
Estimate dead times along flows_to edges from data; confirmed edges are never changed.

Option Type Default Description --data existing file required Historian export, CSV or Parquet, wide or long --graph existing file required Plant graph whose flows_to edges get dead times --max-lag-minutes float 240.0 Longest dead time to search --step-seconds float Grid step (default: the slower tag's median period) --z-threshold float 5.0 Peak strength needed to keep a lag --timezone str UTC Time zone of naive timestamps in the export --in-place bool False Write the estimates back into --graph and log them in its history

items.title: penguineer init
items.text:
Create a project folder for one unit: penguineer.yaml, an empty graph.yaml, folders.

Option Type Default Description --unit str Unit name (default: the folder name) --timezone str UTC Time zone of naive timestamps in exports --force bool False Overwrite an existing penguineer.yaml

items.title: penguineer investigate
items.text:
Align the data in time, rank root-cause hypotheses along graph paths, write the report.

Option Type Default Description --lot str required Lot ID as it appears in the LIMS export --lims existing file required LIMS export --data existing file required Historian export --graph existing file Plant graph (default: graph.yaml in the project) --lots existing file Lot windows: a CSV with lot, start, end (default: from one lab sample of the property to the next) --quality str LIMS property to investigate (default: the lot's worst off-spec one) --top int 5 Hypotheses to report --hops int 6 flows_to hops to search upstream --reference-lots int 3 In-spec lots to compare with --step-seconds float Grid step (default: the slowest candidate tag's period) --timezone str UTC Time zone of naive timestamps in the exports --llm none | local | api none LLM for the prose summary only --llm-model str Model for --llm (default: llm.model in penguineer.yaml) --llm-dry-run bool False Write what would be sent to the LLM, and send nothing --out path Report folder (default: reports/ in the project)

items.title: penguineer lag
items.text:
Fit the actual delay from a cause to an effect: fixed, flow-driven, or with mixing.

Option Type Default Description --data existing file required Historian export, CSV or Parquet, wide or long --cause str required Upstream tag --effect str required Downstream tag, or with --lims a lab property --lims existing file LIMS export: the effect is then a lab property, compared at its sample times --flow str, repeatable Flow tags through the line, summed (enables the flow and volume models) --flow-unit str m3/h Unit of the flow tags, for the volumes --start datetime Window start (inclusive) --end datetime Window end (exclusive) --max-lag-minutes float 240.0 Longest delay to search --step-seconds float Grid step (default: the slower tag's median period) --z-threshold float 5.0 Peak strength needed for an online effect, |corr|·√n --timezone str UTC Time zone of naive timestamps in the exports --out path Folder for the plots (default: the run folder)

items.title: Code layout
items.text:
One repository holds a uv workspace with two Python packages.

packages/plantgraph/      the plant graph schema (depends only on Pydantic)
src/penguineer/
  core/                   command registry, RunContext, run records, errors
  cli/                    the Typer app generated from the registry, the CLI reference renderer
  commands/               one module per command: Params, Result, run()
  io/                     historian, LIMS, plant graph, DEXPI P&ID, Homeostat Live and scenario-bundle readers
  engines/                deterministic engines: data health, dead times, alignment, tests, investigate,
                          and the fitted calibration (calibration.json)
  bench/                  the homeostat bench plant and its faults, bundle export, scoring
  llm/                    optional LLM providers, response cache, versioned prompts
  report/                 report models, grounded summary, evidence plots, HTML and Markdown templates
  graph/                  graph check and graph draft (tag list and P&ID)
tests/                    unit, CLI, round-trip property, schema snapshot and Homeostat Live tests
examples/demo/            a small plant with injected data faults
examples/offspec/         a small plant with an off-spec lot and a known root cause
scripts/                  demo data, Homeostat Live download, CLI reference generator, calibration fit
docs/                     this site

items.title: Run record
items.text:
Every call writes runs/<run_id>/run.json under its project folder, from the CLI or Python and also when it fails. The run ID is a UTC timestamp plus six random hex characters, for example 20261017T195308Z-510ada.

Field What run_id The run ID command The command name, for example data health params The validated params as JSON argv The equivalent command line, from to_argv penguineer_version, plantgraph_version, python_version Versions seed The random seed llm The LLM mode: none, local or api llm_provider, llm_model, llm_prompts The provider (local, anthropic or openai), the model and the prompt versions a run used, when it used an LLM inputs Every input file: path, sha256 and bytes outputs Paths of the files the command wrote started_at, duration_s When it started and how long it took status, exit_code, error ok or error, the exit code and the error message

Alchemist seals the run record into its own run manifest.
